book.title: The account in one page
book.text: Heritage Strategies is a Long Island advisory firm that plans estates for very wealthy families. Its signature deliverable is the Heritage Book, a hand-built set of sheets and diagrams that took 150 to 200 hours per client. Supernal has spent about 18 months turning that book into software, the Heritage Vault, after two earlier attempts were scrapped. Since March 2026 the aim has been larger: Heritage is creating a separate company, Heritage AI Inc., to license the platform to other advisory firms from early 2027. That decision explains nearly everything bought since. Account OS shows six closed deals worth $1,339,985 and three open ones worth $264,000. The app build runs at about $90,000 a month and reaches its contractual threshold of $840,000 in January 2027. Five projects are active: the app, a private cloud environment, two websites and a set of brand videos. The relationship is close and commercially generous, and it is scored 5.0 in Account OS. The same records note that no pilot firm is using the platform, that the client reviews work slowly, and that nobody has agreed what happens in February 2027.

book.title: Why they bought, three times
book.text: The first purchase, in February 2025, is not documented in the sources read here. The second is. By early 2026 the engagement had hit a roadblock. Seb and Jens pulled engineering time and produced a 28-page vision document showing what Heritage could become. The client started resourcing Phase 2 at once, and the Expansion closed on 22 April 2026. Three things worked together: the document made the future concrete, the goal shifted from an internal tool to a licensable product, and the founder wanted an AI-native firm. The third purchase came two months later. Heritage raised $2M to $3M in June. Supernal had just delivered four milestones in one week and, without being asked, proposed an accelerated three-month roadmap. The client said it no longer had the capacity to plan the roadmap itself. The Acceleration closed on 28 June and tripled the pace. Later add-ons each have their own reason: the private environment removes security objections in sales, the videos and websites sell the new company, Foreman frees the founders from office management, and the Insurance CRM replaces a failing system.
sources: Heritage, Ridgeback, Supernal Weekly Call, 17 Aug 2026

book.title: How the deal is built
book.text: There is no single contract. Three order forms stack on one product: $10,000, $14,000 and $66,000 a month, which add to the $90,000 a month the client talks about. That money buys points at $7,500 each, so about 12 a month. Every feature is a numbered order-form item with a point size, and a point is roughly a week of work. When cumulative build spend reaches $840,000, in January 2027, building stops and a maintenance tier begins. Around this core sit separate order forms: the private environment at $7,790 a month, the videos at $32,500, the websites, and two AI employees not yet signed. The model gives the client precise control, and that is also its cost. Heritage calls it death by a thousand cuts. More than half of October's points were additions to the original scope. About 29 to 40 points of wanted work sit beyond the threshold. Ryan proposed a pod subscription to replace points; the team could not find a better control mechanism, parked it, and drafted it again as OF-008. Internally the order-form volume is a running joke.
sources: Heritage Platform Weekly Sync, 26 Aug and 15 Oct 2026

book.title: The product and why it is built this way
book.text: The Vault has five sections: a data sheet, an asset sheet, an insurance schedule, a flow diagram of the estate documents, and an estate distribution chart. Advisers upload documents to a data room. The system labels and routes them, answers a fixed question set for each document type, and maps the answers onto the sheets. Humans check at all three steps, because the team judged human QC the fastest route to the 99.9% accuracy the brand needs. The flow diagram is the differentiator: it colours trust language to show what is fine, what should go and what to use instead. Heritage chose to compete on that visual output and not on drafting documents, where Wealth.com is strong. The licensing goal shapes the rest. Firms are fully separated. White-labelling stops at logo and colour. Seats allow one session at a time. Firms write their own disclosures. Billing features wait until pricing is settled. One weakness surfaced in October: the model learned on documents from top law firms and misreads poorly drafted trusts, which is what licensees will bring.
sources: Heritage Platform Weekly Sync, 13 Aug and 21 Oct 2026

book.title: How delivery has gone
book.text: Delivery began behind. In April 2026 the team was late at 4 points a month, because requirements arrived late and items were scoped too small. Jens became tech lead and engineers were added. July brought a backend migration and a company-wide security incident that froze deployments. From August the pace held, but friction moved to the client side: updates were too technical, staff emailed requests directly, and finished work sat untested. Each complaint produced a rule: plain-English definitions, requests through Chris and Tom Jr., testers named before release, updates grouped by what matters to book production. By late October the team reported its best app week, with multi-tenancy and secure access in production. Yet only 2 of October's 12 points were closed by 30 October, and on 9 November six items sat in review. Turning 2FA on in production locked clients out and was reverted the same day. The private environment was promised in two weeks when engineering expected months; the agreed position is two weeks for the Vertex move and six to eight weeks for the full migration.
sources: Delivery Team Sync, 20 Apr and 4 May 2026
Heritage, Ridgeback, Supernal Weekly Call, 10 and 31 Aug 2026
Heritage Platform Weekly Sync, 26 Aug and 2 Sep 2026
Account OS health note, week of 26 Oct 2026

book.title: The people
book.text: Tom Fanning Sr. founded the firm and sets the deadlines. He wants numbers and trackers, and he tends to get pulled into detail on the weekly calls, which is why a quarterly forum for him was proposed. Tom Fanning Jr. makes product decisions and pushes toward what licensees and families will value. Chris Halvey holds the budget and the contracts, owns the insurance sheet, and is the person who notices when an order form is late. Below them, directors each own a sheet: Keith the diagrams, Willie the assets, Lisa onboarding. Jess runs operations. Ridgeback's Brendan and Eric are meant to bring pilot firms and have been slow. On Supernal's side the account has changed hands. Chris sold the first deal. Seb led through the vision document. Sven grew from project manager into strategist and now carries the vision. Jens runs daily delivery and most client calls. Ryan sponsors and owns the deals but has said he was not managing the account strategically. Stuart joined in October to take the commercial side. The team worried about adding another face.

book.title: What value has shown
book.text: The headline claim to prospects is a book in about 30 minutes instead of 150 to 200 hours, with accuracy up from about 50% to about 99%. The measured picture is more modest and more useful. A timed run in September took 75 minutes for four insurance policies. The October baseline is 16.5 hours per book, of which sheet QC is 34% and client onboarding 30%. Stage accuracy on the dashboard mock-up was 87.3% for routing, 97.2% for answers and about 89% for mapping, against a need for 95% at every stage before full automation. Monthly time tracking began on 28 October so that a falling trend can be shown. Commercial value to Heritage AI is still a forecast: zero revenue in 2026, about $1.25M targeted for 2027. Value to Supernal is clear. Heritage is about 40% of revenue, the reference for the points model, and the source of the private-cloud capability and the new marketing services line.
sources: Platform testing, timing, and accuracy, 9 Sep 2026
Heritage Platform Weekly Sync, 26 Aug and 28 Oct 2026

book.title: Where it stands and what is next
book.text: Three things decide the next quarter. First, the commercial cliff. The build threshold arrives in January 2027 with about 3 contracted points left, 29 or more points of wanted work beyond it, and no agreed model for February. The options on the table are maintenance at $35,417 a month plus features on top, or a pod. Heritage wants to stay near $90,000 a month only while it uses the capacity. Second, proof. No pilot firm is live. Portals for Ridgeback's firms are being set up, the demo vault is nearly ready, and Heritage plans to invite 50 of its own clients. Until a firm outside Heritage uses the product, the licensing story rests on demos. Third, promises with dates: the private environment on 16 November, two websites on 20 November that are gated on a trademark filing not yet started, video cuts in early December, and two order forms to sign before Thanksgiving. The visit to New York in early November showed that time in the room moves this client faster than calls.
sources: Heritage Platform Weekly Sync, 15 and 21 Oct 2026

answers.q: What happens to revenue after January 2027?
answers.a: The app build reaches its $840K threshold in January 2027 with about 3 contracted points left. No model for February is agreed: options are maintenance at $35,417 a month plus features, or a pod subscription. Heritage wants to stay near $90K a month only while it uses the capacity.

answers.q: Why is health 5.0 when the notes say yellow?
answers.a: Account OS has scored every dimension 5.0 for six weeks, but the same records note that no pilot firm is using the platform. Notion’s 2 to 9 Nov report opens “Yellow” because items are not closing. The score and the notes have not been reconciled.

answers.q: What would prove the licensing story?
answers.a: A firm outside Heritage using the product. Portals for Ridgeback’s firms are being set up, the demo vault is nearly ready, and Heritage plans to invite 50 of its own clients. Until then the story rests on demos.
